title: Dilucidationes super methodo elegantissima, qua illustris de la Grange usus est in integranda aequatione differentiali dx/√X = dy/√Y

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E506 explains Lagrange's method for integrating dx/√X + dy/√Y = 0. Euler first tests it on the simpler separable equation dx/(a+2bx+cx²) + dy/(a+2by+cy²) = 0. The method introduces a parameter t, passes to second differentials, and adds and subtracts the two equations. In §§18–19 it yields the first integral

(a+2bx+cx²)(a+2by+cy²)/(a−cxy)² = C,

or, after subtracting 1,

[2ab(x+y) + ac(x+y)² + 4b²xy + 2bcxy(x+y)]/(a−cxy)² = C.

This page checks that integral against the classical integrals obtained from the arctangent addition formula.

§20 end (a=1, b=0, c=1): the formula gives (x+y)²/(1−xy)² = C. This is equivalent to (x+y)/(1−xy) = C, which is tan(arctan x + arctan y).

§21 (a=1, b=1/2, c=1): the equation is dx/(1+x+x²) + dy/(1+y+y²) = 0.
- Euler integrates directly: ∫dx/(1+x+x²) = (2/√3) arctan(x√3/(2+x)). This differs from the usual form (2/√3) arctan((2x+1)/√3) only by the constant (2/√3)(π/6).
- The tangent addition formula then gives arctan[2√3(x+y+xy)/(4+2(x+y)−2xy)] = C, hence (x+y+xy)/(2+x+y−xy) = C.
- The Lagrange-type formula gives [x+y+(x+y)²+xy+xy(x+y)]/(1−xy)² = C. This factors as (1+x+y)(x+y+xy)/(1−xy)² = C.
- To reconcile the two, Euler inverts the first integral and subtracts 1. This gives (2−2xy)/(x+y+xy); he drops the harmless factor 2 and writes (1−xy)/(x+y+xy) = C.
- Multiplying this into the factored form gives (1+x+y)/(1−xy) = C.

§22: Euler sets α = (1−xy)/(x+y+xy) and β = (1+x+y)/(1−xy). On the next page he notes the identity β − 1/α = 1, so the two integrals are functionally dependent ('pulcherrimus consensus'). He then generalizes the factorization to [2b+c(x+y)][a(x+y)+2bxy]/(a−cxy)². This leads to the reduction to the simplest integral (2b+c(x+y))/(a−cxy) = C. In modern terms, the second-order Lagrange procedure produced a function of the true invariant: Q = (aP−2b)/c, so PQ = (aP²−2bP)/c.
errors: No substantive errors; I verified every algebraic step.
In 'vnitate subtracta' the result is actually 2(1−xy)/(x+y+xy); Euler silently drops the factor 2, which is legitimate since C is arbitrary.
Passing from arctan(...)=C to the tangent argument = C is valid modulo the usual branch/π issues, which are irrelevant here.

ideas.what: Integrating dx/(1+x+x²) as (2/√3)·arctan(x√3/(2+x)) and combining two such terms by the tangent addition formula into an algebraic first integral
ideas.modern_name: Addition theorem for the arctangent / algebraic integral of a separable Riccati-type equation
ideas.where_published: Institutiones calculi integralis (E342/E366) and many Euler papers on dx/X + dy/Y = 0

ideas.what: Checking the integral produced by Lagrange's second-differential method against the known integral, by factoring it and showing the two are functionally dependent (β − 1/α = 1)
ideas.modern_name: Functional dependence of first integrals; the integral as a function of a projective invariant
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, this paper (commentary on Lagrange, Misc. Taurinensia c. 1766–69)
ideas.where_published: E506 itself (Acta Acad. Sci. Petrop. 1778, publ. 1781)

ideas.modern_name: Symmetric biquadratic / Möbius-invariant form of the addition law for quadratic X
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (degenerate case of the Euler addition theorem for elliptic integrals)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine verification of Lagrange's method on quadratic X using the arctangent addition formula; it is correct and already published in E506, with nothing absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image; only the long-s forms (ſ) are normalized.
In §21 the image reads 'b = 1/2' (printed as a small fraction), consistent with the transcription.
